articles.title: Supreme Court rulings have been 'destructive to our democracy,' Justice Kagan says
articles.summary: By Jan Wolfe WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said the court's conservative majority has undermined democracy and "created a race to the bottom" in how congressional districts are drawn. Kagan, one of the court's ‌three liberals, told students at Catholic University's law school that the conservatives have enabled increased political polarization by not reining ‌in partisan gerrymandering, which involves states redrawing the boundaries of electoral districts based on the partisan leanings of voters to boost a political party's candidates. In recent years, Kagan ​said, "both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality." Partisan gerrymandering is driving political candidates "toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about anymore is being primaried," Kagan said. "It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. "In this election, and ‌the next election, we are seeing large states ⁠with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is ⁠very destructive to our democracy." The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, in April gutted a pillar of the Voting Rights Act, a landmark 1965 civil rights law that aimed to prevent racial discrimination in voting. That ruling prompted a frenzied round of redistricting across the South to eliminate US House ​of ​Representatives districts where Black voters make up a majority or near-majority, as ​Republican-led states scrambled to take advantage of the decision. ‌President Donald Trump's Republican Party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. At Trump's urging, Republican-governed Texas redrew its electoral map last year in an effort to flip Democratic-held US House seats, while Democratic-led California then reconfigured its map to target Republican-held House seats. Kagan, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, said the court's conservatives did not appreciate the real-world impact of their April voting rights decision, or their June decision that struck down a cap on the amount of money parties can spend on campaigns with ‌input from candidates. "I think part of the reason why the court got it ​wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences ​of their decisions," Kagan said. “I do think in all these ​areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political ‌system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t ​work as well as it should,” ​she added. Kagan added that the June decision on campaign finance regulation has created opportunities for donors to corrupt candidates. "The one place where the court has allowed campaign finance regulation to operate is to prevent quid pro quo corruption, kind of money ​for favors, and the court never seems to ‌see the opportunities for doing exactly that," Kagan said. “I think you know the people of America look around this political ​system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she ​said. (Reporting by Jan Wolfe; Editing by Andrew Chung and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-high-court-rulings-destructive-013650423.html

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, sources say
articles.summary: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week. Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine. It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X . Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order. The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications. Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown. "I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service. "We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success." Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service. What is Starshield? Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink. The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close. What happened in Ukraine? Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones. The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things." Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored." The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week. "There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend . Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed? Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S. , and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine." Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week. Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/elon-musk-ukraine-spacex-starshield-trump-administration/

articles.title: Ohio governor candidate hits back after estranged mother appears in attack ad
articles.summary: Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's campaign slammed her GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy Tuesday, alleging his campaign used her estranged mother, whom she has accused of abusing her and standing by the man who sexually abused her, to urge voters not to support her in the toss-up race. A video that appears to be a campaign ad circulated on social media late Monday showing Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, saying that she loves her daughter, but adds, "Amy has a serious problem" and has lied about her past. ABC News has not been able to verify the content or authenticity of the video, which has been shared by many users online, including Donald Trump Jr. Stephen Zenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images - PHOTO: Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health and Democratic gubernatorial candidate, speaks on affordability while campaigning at Bottoms Up Coffee in Columbus, Ohio, April 6, 2026. Ramaswamy told reporters on Tuesday that the ad did come from his campaign and that he viewed it as "legitimate." He said that Acton's mother was not compensated. "It is an ad from our campaign, and the thing that I want to say is that I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans, and unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues. She won't debate me," he said. In the campaign ad, Arthur describes her daughter as a "liar," saying, "She lies about her past." "My daughter needs help, and she can't help you if she needs help herself," Arthur says in the video. Arthur couldn't immediately be reached for comment. Deadline passes for embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller to drop off ballot Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, criticized Ramaswamy over the "disgusting attack." "It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point," Stearns said in a statement. "After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," he added. Ohio gubernatorial candidate speaks out after man arrested for alleged confrontation at fair This is not the first time Arthur has publicly accused her daughter of lying. In an interview with an anti-abortion access group in 2020, Arthur accused Acton's father of convincing their daughter to lie. When asked earlier Tuesday if the ad was made with the campaign's knowledge or consent, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, released a lengthy statement Tuesday, but did not deny making the ad or denounce it. "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor," Luck said in a statement. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks during the Darke County Republican Party Hog Roast on October 18, 2026 in Greenville, Ohio. Luck's statement went on to accuse Acton of "lying about Vivek and his family, lying about her own record, and then hiding from debates," and questioning her actions during the pandemic when she was the director of the Ohio Department of Health. "If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves. The fact that she won't, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who's really lying," Luck ended her statement. Acton pushed back in an interview with Spectrum News Tuesday. "I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is something I'm just complaining about. Who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect and sexual abuse; my brother and I were removed," she said. The campaign released a video ad later Tuesday where Stearns echoed his criticism over Ramaswamy "Shame on Vivek,” he says, adding, "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio. He's not fit to lead." Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and seeking therapy for it, She has also openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother. In an interview with the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019, when she was first appointed director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton described a childhood that was "out of control", shuffling between houses with her mother and brother and the "cast of characters" her mother dated. She alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. Jeff Swensen/Getty Images - PHOTO: Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Governor of Ohio, greets constituents along the parade route of the 54th Annual CDC Parade on September 7, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. A newspaper article from August 1978 corroborates Acton's account. The article in the Youngstown Vindicator describes that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was "bound over to the Mahoning County grand jury in connection with the rape of a 12-year-old girl." Acton was born in 1966, making her 12 at the time. The article says he was "arrested at his home on August 4 th following an investigation initiated by the girl's father." Cledith Arthur died in 2004. He and Acton's mother remained married after the allegations. "In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton said in the 2019 interview about her mother. "I was lucky that it got bad enough, because it got me out of there." Midterm candidates dumping debates: 'There's no reason to get up there and argue about differences of opinion' Acton's father received custody, which she credited for turning her life around. She then graduated top of her class in high school, was homecoming queen, and became a doctor. Ramaswamy has also been criticized for making comments seen as dismissive of his opponents' experiences, saying that Acton "only ever talks about something that happened to her" rather than having a positive message. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/amy-acton-campaign-slams-ramaswamy-controversial-ad-featuring/story?id=137421475

articles.title: Musk opens the door to a SpaceX-Tesla merger as shareholders weigh a deal
articles.summary: Elon Musk's rocket and AI company posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period (Kent NISHIMURA) Elon Musk said Tuesday he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms. Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea." Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments. Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders. He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest. Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX. He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares. He holds about 20 percent of Tesla. The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty. Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle." He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing. His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street. SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion. Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million. The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI. The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales. - Cloud computing - SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup. SpaceX’s cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centers. Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029. The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier. As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy. SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion. Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier. Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027. That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year. He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor." Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69 percent to $5.2 billion, and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million. Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 from $83 a year earlier. SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale. The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit. arp/mlm This article originally appeared on AFP at https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/musk-says-backs-spacex-tesla-220507985.html

articles.title: Trump unveils fraud whistleblower rewards, but he gets to decide who gets paid
articles.summary: Washington — President Trump on Tuesday announced the federal government will compensate whistleblowers who report people defrauding the U.S. government and taxpayers, but said he will decide who gets paid. "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," the president said during his Oval Office announcement with Vice President JD Vance, who heads up the administration's fraud task force, beside him. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving and I'll determine — and I will be very generous, believe me." Through the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, Mr. Trump said whistleblowers, who can be ordinary citizens, will be eligible to receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, even if the reported fraud is $100 billion. America.gov/fraud , however, says successful whistleblowers will be paid up to $30,000, dependent upon the report resulting in criminal charges. Asked by CBS News for clarification, Mr. Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, and criminal charges aren't necessary. "That's the answer. I quit while I'm ahead," Vance joked. The president promised to be "fair" in his decisions. "You'll get your money immediately, but I'll make the determination," he continued. "So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they'll split it or maybe whatever, but I'll make that determination." The America.gov/fraud website says reports are encrypted and will go directly to the Treasury Department. It's not immediately clear who reviews reports, although the Department of Justice will administer the program. The first person to benefit from the program is Nick Shirley , a 20-something YouTuber who published a video alleging fraud at childcare centers in Minnesota. He stood alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday and was presented with a $10,000 check. Some whistleblowers can already receive compensation from the False Claims Act, which allows some whistleblowers to be entitled to up to 25% to 30% of proceeds recovered. But the requirements are stringent. Vance said "99%" of the fraud they're finding isn't covered by the False Claims Act. Naomi Seligman, president of nonprofit Whistleblower Aid, was skeptical of Mr. Trump's announcement, saying the president "is more interested in hunting down whistleblowers." "If the president is truly interested in rooting out wrongdoing, Whistleblower Aid invites him to start by examining the violations perpetrated by his own administration, including senior officials," she said in a statement. "We would happily work with him on this vital accountability effort to help save our democracy." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-us-compensate-fraud-whistleblowers/

articles.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
articles.summary: Monday's lawsuit filed by "Jane Doe"  alleges that a member of Alpha Delta Phi sexually assaulted her during a fraternity party on Feb. 7.  (E. Jason Wambsgans / Chicago Tribune via Getty) A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses. The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants. “The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.” Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago. The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation. “These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.” Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.” “The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.” Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization. Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university. Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit. She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.” “I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.” She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.” The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says. The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances. “I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News. The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says. After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her. Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on. She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night. The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report. Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report. Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit. A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case. Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs. Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university. The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case. “At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/woman-sexually-assaulted-fraternity-university-chicago-lawsuit-alleges-rcna604607

articles.title: Trump says Russia 'has been fine on Ukraine' as he makes deals with Putin
articles.summary: A series of Trump administration moves over the last two weeks — including decisions to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and delay other measures targeting the Russian economy — have led both Republicans and Democrats to question whether President Trump is changing course and siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the war between their two countries. "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump told reporters on Monday. "They haven't been doing much." In contrast, the president continued, "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that." Russia and Ukraine have been at war for more than 12 years. But in February 2022, the conflict entered a new, deadlier phase when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and tried to seize territory. The fighting has since become a grinding war of attrition. The United States has generally supported Ukraine, even as direct military aid has waned during Trump's second term . The administration's latest steps, however, "amount to a major reversal in U.S. strategy," the New York Times reported on Sunday . "The breach with Ukraine has been sudden and perhaps irreparable." So what's going on here? Posting Sunday on social media , Trump defended his actions by insisting that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" and doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine, he said, is targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which is "hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." He said that "farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World." But even Republicans have pushed back. "I think it's clear Russia is the aggressor, and we've got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia," GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida told the Associated Press over the weekend. "So it's not the first thing I would be doing." When Zelensky was asked last week if he believed Ukraine was "losing" the U.S., he replied: "Yes." "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," Zelensky said. On Tuesday, Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo , Norway. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, participated via video link. On Wednesday, Witkoff and Kushner will reportedly fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Putin in his hometown with "an updated set of [peace] proposals," according to the BBC. Is a diplomatic breakthrough in the offing? Here's what you need to know about the latest developments. What's changed in recent days Oct. 9: Trump said he had reached an agreement with Putin to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets. Minutes later, the Treasury Department announced that it would be lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027. Those sanctions — which limited Putin's ability to bankroll the invasion of Ukraine — have been in place since 2022. "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" the president wrote on social media. Oct. 10: Trump blamed Zelensky for high U.S. diesel prices and said Ukraine should replace him. "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump told reporters before leaving for a campaign rally in Tennessee . "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does." Oct. 11: On social media, Trump declared an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine." He claimed that "both parties have agreed." Zelensky said the agreement was news to him , but added that he would be willing to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries if Russia pauses attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and other energy infrastructure in return. Oct. 11-14: For three days, Zelensky held his fire on Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Putin continued to bombard Ukraine's energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power ahead of winter. The Trump administration clarified that its "energy ceasefire" applied solely to attacks on oil refineries , but Ukraine doesn't have any fully operational oil refineries — Russia has repeatedly attacked and disabled the last one in recent years. Oct. 14: Ukraine discovered that its access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network — as well as Starshield, its military-grade counterpart — had been throttled , limiting its ability to defend itself from Russian ballistic missile attacks on energy infrastructure. "Right at the moment Trump was warning Zelensky not to attack Russian refineries, the Starshield settings were somehow altered, such that the system could not track objects traveling at speeds greater than about 100 miles per hour — woefully inadequate to detect Russian aerial assaults," the National Review explained . Citing four sources familiar with the discussions, the Telegraph reported that "Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine" and that Trump "agreed." In response, Trump denied any involvement, saying, "I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon." Musk wrote on social media that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Reuters also reported that the "order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside [the] White House." The Wall Street Journal reported this week that “Elon Musk ordered the slowdown” — “a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration.” Oct. 15: Zelensky said that Ukraine would resume attacking Russian oil refineries. "That's it," Zelensky told the Financial Times . "The block is out. We're done." Oct. 16: Trump issued an executive order waiving new sanctions against Russia — as well as tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy — that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act that he signed in September. "I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," Trump told Newsmax . "I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin." Oct. 18: Trump wrote on social media that his "decision on Russia is a very simple one" aimed at striking a peace deal and lowering energy costs for Americans. "Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," Trump claimed, saying that he doesn't  "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." He continued, "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way." In contrast, Trump claimed Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." Oct. 19: Citing "a U.S. official and three additional people familiar with the situation," the Washington Post reported that the Trump administration is holding up "the transfer of interceptor missiles to Ukraine that are needed to protect the country from Russian missile and drone attacks." Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky again, saying, "It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Oct. 20: Witkoff and Kushner met with Zelensky in Oslo. According to the BBC , Zelensky suggested after the meeting that "crucial issues of early warning of Russia's ballistic missile strikes had… been resolved." Zelensky also said that he discussed Ukraine's access to missiles and Starlink with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio — and he expected "good results." Will Trump's deals with Putin lower U.S. diesel prices? Trump has accused Zelensky of "knowing that these attacks" on Russian refineries "are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." It's true that the price of diesel is up about 77% so far this year — putting it near record highs and raising costs for American farmers, truckers and businesses (which in turn puts upward pressure on the price of consumer goods and services). But energy analysts say the Iran War, not Ukrainian attacks on Russia, is the major reason diesel is so much more expensive than it used to be. "The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz, that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," one recently told the New York Times . In 2025, Russian diesel exports accounted for roughly 9% of the global diesel trade — or about 700,000 barrels a day, according to S&P Global Energy. That number has fallen to about 140,000 barrels a day since Ukraine started targeting Russian oil refineries. Trump's deal with Putin would amount to another 75,000 barrels a day, according to the New York Times . That's not nothing — but experts say it's also not enough to make a huge price difference in the U.S. To put those 75,000 barrels in perspective, diesel exports from Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries have fallen by 800,000 barrels per day since the start of the Iran war in February. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, estimated in an Oct. 9 social media post that Trump's deal with Russia could eventually lower the cost of diesel by 10 to 20 cents per gallon. Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, likened the impact to "putting a Band-Aid on a gunshot wound." And that's assuming Russia can deliver. According to the Times, "many analysts consider [even] those numbers to be unrealistic because roughly 40 to 50 percent of Russian refining capacity is offline" — and "repairing and restarting refineries can take months or years in the best of circumstances." Trump has been taking various steps to try to lower U.S. gas prices ahead of November's midterm elections, including signing an executive order allowing tax-free purchases of red-dyed off-road diesel. But an October AP poll found that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of how the president is handling the cost of living — and 65% now blame his policies for persistently high prices more than factors beyond his control. Will Trump's deals with Putin end the war? On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright described Trump's diesel deal as a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine. It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC News . The Times has also reported that the "Trump administration's talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner." "The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia's biggest energy companies," the paper added. Meanwhile, at their talks in Oslo on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner were expected to tell Zelensky that "holding out to retain occupied portions of the country's eastern provinces is not worth it — and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia's terms," according to the Times . In short, the Trump administration appears to be pushing harder than ever before to force Ukraine to cede sovereign territory to Russia as part of a negotiated end to the war. Whether Zelensky succumbs to that pressure remains to be seen. "I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," he told Bloomberg in an interview published on Sunday . "I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks." "If the United States will support Putin — it's unbelievable, it's a tragedy," Zelensky added Sunday on NBC News's Meet the Press . "If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand." articles.title: U.S. is reportedly nearing a deal with Russia to free multiple jailed Americans
articles.summary: The Trump administration is closing in on a deal with Moscow that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter tell ABC News. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner have been leading the negotiations, which are said to be in the final stages, according to the sources. With Gilman's release from Russia, families of other detained Americans hope their relatives will be next They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges. Moscow City Court Press Service via AP - PHOTO: In this Oct. 7, 2024, file photo released by the Moscow City Court Press Service, Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine against Russia stands in a glass cage during a court session in Moscow. However, officials caution that while the terms of the arrangement are coming into focus, nothing has been finalized and it’s still possible it won’t materialize or that its scope will change. Asked about a potential deal to free Hubbard on Tuesday, Trump said he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it "at length" and called for Hubbard's return to the U.S. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens. OK, let's see what happens. I'd love to get him back. It's time. It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back," Trump said in the Oval Office. News of the potential deal comes as Witkoff is expected to present Putin with a proposal for a partial ceasefire covering energy and food infrastructure, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Tuesday. Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at a news briefing in Oslo, Norway, following talks with Witkoff. On Monday, Trump spoke about his dealings with Russia, saying he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time," presumably referring to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon." Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy On Tuesday, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov was asked about a potential prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. "Dialogue on all these issues is ongoing through intelligence service channels," he said. Ryabkov added that Hubbard's name was "certainly familiar," but said he had "nothing to report" on the matter. Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Jan. 10, 2022, file photo, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov looks on during a press conference following talks with US counterpart on soaring tensions over Ukraine, in Geneva. The White House declined to comment on the matter. It's not clear what Russia might receive in exchange for releasing U.S. citizens. However, Trump has made multiple policy decisions viewed as favorable to Moscow in recent days, including waiving newly imposed sanctions targeting Russian officials and oligarchs mandated by a bill Trump signed into law last month after it passed by wide margins in Congress. Trump has also increased pressure on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy sites. There are currently at least eight American citizens and two dual U.S.-Russia nationals detained by Moscow: Hubbard, Gordon Black, Michael Leake, Robert Woodland, David Barnes, Daniel Schneider, Andre Khachatorrian, Chuck Zimmerman, Alexsandor Antonov and Eugene Spector. Families of the incarcerated Americans in Russia have called for the State Department to extend more wrongful detention designations, with Leake's family renewing its request in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, saying Leake was "left behind" in the Aug. 1, 2024, prisoner trade. ABC New s ' Catherine Bouvet contributed to thi s report. articles.title: Trump administration freezes another $1.2 billion in California Medicaid payments
articles.summary: Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator, speaks Tuesday in the Oval Office as President Trump and Nick Shirley listen. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) The Trump administration is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California, citing concerns about potential fraud in a state program that helps older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said federal officials took action after they grew concerned about the rapid expansion of California’s personal care services program in recent years. State officials were notified of the decision Tuesday, he said. “California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said. “Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California.” Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud but suggested the state was paying people too much taxpayer money to help with services that could be offered for free, like “paying somebody to carry groceries upstairs for your mom.” “Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said. Read more: Vance says $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments to California will be deferred over fraud concerns The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California. In May, the administration held back $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to the state over concerns about “fraudsters” in the state’s hospice and in-home care programs. The actions have been part of a broad effort by the administration to rein in fraud in federal healthcare benefits programs, particularly in Democrat-led states. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla criticized the administration’s decision. “This Administration’s track record speaks for itself: Fewer people have health insurance, premiums are up, and drug costs are higher. This decision will hurt older Californians, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or injury,” Padilla said in a statement. “The American people deserve better, and I’ll keep fighting against their attacks.” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the office has been critical of the administration’s past efforts. In May, Newsom’s office called the action to withhold funds for in-home care programs a “sick” and politically motivated attack on services that are meant to “keep seniors and people with disabilities OUT of nursing homes.” Those services usually cover assistants who help people with daily tasks such as bathing, laundry or cooking. They also provide needed care such as injections under the direction of a medical professional. A 2020 report by the California state auditor found that nearly three-quarters of In-home Supportive Services caregivers assist a family member. Newsom’s office, however, has argued that the program saves taxpayers money, saying IHSS care costs $30,000 a year, while nursing home care costs $137,000 a year. Read more: Medicaid reckoning awaits next California governor after program’s rapid expansion California’s hospice industry has had problems in the past and authorities have tried to crack down on the issue. A Times investigation in 2020 found that providers were billing Medicare for hospice services and equipment for patients who were not actually dying while the industry boomed. The Trump administration, led by Vice President JD Vance, has tried to focus attention on the issue of waste, fraud and abuse as a centerpiece policy platform to bring down healthcare costs. On Tuesday, Trump and Vance announced a $25-million whistleblower program designed to pay out cash to people who tip off the federal government about fraudsters. The program will offer a 1% commission for tips that lead to a successful conviction. Trump said he would be the sole arbitrator of who gets to keep the money. “I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.” Trump said the money will be handed out “expeditiously and fairly.” “I promise there is nothing in this for me,” he said. The White House referred comment about the decision to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Get the L.A. Times California Politics newsletter. Deeply reported insights into legislation, politics and policy from Sacramento, Washington and beyond, in your inbox twice per week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/feds-hold-back-additional-1-203302354.html

articles.title: New details emerge about dad who stopped Oregon school shooter within minutes
articles.summary: More details have emerged about the "hero" bystander who intervened within minutes of a gunman opening fire at an elementary school in Oregon. Kaylub Giamanco, 36, fatally shot the 16-year-old gunman who killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15. His actions "undoubtedly saved people," police said. Giamanco, a carpenter and father of two girls who attend Silver Rail Elementary, had gone through "military shooting drills" with veterans who fought in Iraq, The Guardian reported. Seeing the shooting unfold, Giamanco "pursued" gunman Griffin J. John II, his mother, Kenda Freeman, told CBS News . Freeman said the experience has left her son traumatized. "I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives." "Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," Freeman said. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army crawled through the window." Giamanco, who legally owns and carries his weapon, doesn't wish to speak about the school shooting because he feels "riddled with guilt" for not being able to save more lives, his brother, Kyle Giamanco, told the New York Post . A teacher in the classroom had already thrown her cellphone at John, tackled him and fought him, police said. She was not injured. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said her actions likely prevented more bloodshed. Giamanco then fired at John multiple times with a legally owned .40-caliber pistol, killing him just before police arrived, officials said. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek  praised the Bend resident at a press conference, without naming him, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Addressing him directly, she acknowledged the toll it had taken on him. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well." "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage," Krantz said Friday, speaking about the teacher and the man who shot the gunman. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Gun used 'purchased as a birthday gift' The gun used by the 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II was purchased by his mother as a birthday gift, according to reports. The Maverick 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by the mother of the gunman who carried out the shooting, and given to him for recreational use, sources told CBS News . On Friday, two senior law enforcement officials told NBC News that John's mother bought the shotgun and has been cooperating with investigators. The shooter killed Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher from Bend, along with two other children aged 8 and 11 on Thursday. Police said all of the shots were fired inside a single special needs classroom. In an interview with CNN on Sunday, John's mother said that "there were no warning signs" and wouldn't comment on how her son got access to the gun used in the shooting. Schools remain closed Schools across Bend., Ore., will stay closed Monday and Tuesday as the community mourns four people killed on Thursday, when police say a 16-year-old former student opened fire in a special education classroom. Students return Wednesday on an early-release schedule, and Silver Rail will remain closed until further notice, the Bend Bulletin reported . In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued.  "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Megan Lambert, 25, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., was killed in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. Bend Police Department The shooter was identified as Griffin J. John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians confirmed Saturday that John was an enrolled member, NBC News reported . A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving care at the scene was in serious but stable condition at Oregon Health & Science University, police said. A 54-year-old teacher, Becky Drury of Bend, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Bend. Her family allowed police to release her name. Becky Drury, 54, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, was injured in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Her husband, Will Drury, said her left arm "took a lot of damage" and that her right hand also needed surgery, CNN reported . The two other children killed, both boys, were 8 and 11. Their families asked police not to release their names. Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. Police had initially said that the three children who were killed and the one who was injured were the only students in the classroom at the time of the shooting. But on Monday, they confirmed that a fifth student had been present.  That student was "physically unharmed by the assailant," a spokesman for the school district told the Oregonian . A fourth adult, a special education staff member who was also unharmed, was also in the room, police said. Investigators have searched John's home and plan to keep control of the school until at least Tuesday to finish collecting evidence, police said. They are asking anyone with video of a teenage boy in black clothing and a black backpack near Third Street, Brosterhous Road or the school between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Thursday to submit it. The FBI has set up a tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI and fbi.gov/silverrailschool . 'Rhoam was so so strong' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Rhoam Summer's parents, Kelik and Lillian, released a new statement on Monday through their attorneys providing more details on who he was and how best to honor his memory. "Rhoam was so so strong. The day he was born, his father gave him his first sink bath at the hospital. In the sink, Rhoam grabbed his dad's hands and pulled himself up with his own strength. He climbed a ladder (3 step stool) when he was just 6 months old. He never stopped moving. He never stopped climbing. He could do anything," they wrote in the statement shared by the law firm Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss. A GoFundMe set up by friends of the family, one of 10 fundraisers that the site has verified to support those connected to the shooting, has raised more than $187,000 as of Tuesday. In their statement, the Summers said another way to remember Rhoam is to embody the spirit he lived with. "If people want to memorialize our little Rhoam, we request you draw. Sharks, dinosaurs, monsters... Rhoam loved to tell stories of creatures with big teeth who needed understanding and friendship. Please make art for him. Draw or paint. Use your hands if you can. Get messy," they wrote. Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss is one of three law firms the Summers have reportedly hired to "preserve and protect Rhoam's memory and investigate possible legal claims arising from the mass school shooting," according to the Salem Statesman Journal . "Senseless, barbaric, and depraved? Yes. But was it foreseeable and thus preventable?" Tim Williams, cocounsel on the investigation, told the paper. "That's what we will find out. While law enforcement handles the criminal prosecution, we will be investigating any systemic failures that may have allowed this tragedy to happen. We are committed to holding all responsible parties accountable to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again and justice is done in Rhoam's name." articles.title: 机器人产业追踪：Optimus 准备大规模量产，OpenAI 也要做机器人
articles.summary: 特斯拉在2026年股东大会委托书里首次书面宣称Optimus 已"为大规模量产做好准备"，但同一份文件没有给出任何产量、价格与交付日期；OpenAI则在播客里确认自研人形机器人，时间锚点是2027年的演示原型。 人形机器人已经跨过"能不能做出来"，进入了"能不能便宜、稳定、成批地做出来"的阶段，这个阶段的胜负手不在算法，更可能在关节、在良率、在长三角两小时配送圈。当期全球年出货仅约5万台，但估值已经按2030年出货量定价，产业的前瞻式定价成为最大的桎梏之一。

articles.title: 3个月，5个“门外汉”，20万美元预算，Claude加持！“网红研究所”Citrini设计出了“抗蝎毒蛋白”
articles.summary: 一个被忽视的行业，一群门外汉，一个35页提示词，一万小时H100，一张实验室账单，211个蛋白设计，17个阳性结果。 故事从投资问题开始，落在了试管里的新蛋白上。 “网红研究所”Citrini Research最初想搞清楚的是一个投资问题：AI制药到底走到哪一步了？ 过去几年，生命科学和医疗板块经历了明显降温。疫情红利退潮，融资环境收紧，二级市场估值回落，一级市场出手谨慎。相比之下，AI基础设施、半导体、算力链成了更热的叙事。生物医药这个曾经被资本追逐的赛道，开始显得有些冷清。 但Citrini看到的机会也在这里： 如果一个被市场冷落的行业，真的被AI工具改造，那么增长预期可能被低估。 问题在于，没人能给他们一个统一答案。问科学家，有人说AI还没做出过真正重要的新药；也有人认为AI会在几年内重塑药物研发体系。对一家投资研究机构来说，这种分裂判断很难变成投资结论。 于是，他们决定亲自下场。 团队只有5个人，其中3个几乎没有生命科学背景，另外2个有一点相关经验，也谈不上药物研发老兵。预算20万美元，时间3个月。他们给自己定了一个听上去很冒险的目标：借助Claude，设计一种真实可合成、可测试的新蛋白。 如果实验室结果能证明它有效结合目标，哪怕只跨出第一步，也足以说明一件事：AI for Science的门槛正在下降，门外汉也开始有机会进入过去高度专业化的科学发现流程。 一个投资团队，为什么盯上蝎毒？ Citrini一开始没有直接选择蝎毒。他们先列出几个筛选条件：实验验证要快，成本要可控；问题本身要依赖分子设计能力；最好还有现实公共健康价值，同时长期缺少投入。 候选方向包括罕见儿童疾病、艰难梭菌感染、阻断强效芬太尼类似物的“疫苗”、降低莱姆病风险的抗蜱方案。最后留下来的方向，是抗毒血清。 蛇毒方向此前已有AI蛋白设计案例。Citrini想找一个更新、更少被关注的目标，于是把视线转向蝎毒。 蝎子蜇伤并非小众问题。全球每年约有120万人被蝎子蜇伤，数千人死亡，儿童尤其危险。很多高发地区医疗资源有限，抗毒血清价格高、供应不稳定。 现有抗蝎毒血清生产方式相当传统：采集蝎毒，向马体内注入受控剂量，等待马产生抗体，再从血浆中提取和纯化。流程耗时、昂贵，还依赖动物。 Citrini想试一条新路：直接设计一种小蛋白，让它像“分子夹子”一样抓住蝎毒中的神经毒素。这类小蛋白被称为minibinder，体积比抗体更小，理论上可通过合成生物学方式生产。对一个预算有限、时间有限的团队来说，蛋白设计更贴近当前AI能力边界。 他们最终选定5种蝎毒神经毒素，覆盖墨西哥、巴西、北非和中东等地区代表性毒素。最初目标很朴素：先设计出能结合单一毒素的蛋白。只要体外实验能证明“抓得住”，就已经是重要信号。 随后，团队又加了一道更难的题：能否设计一个单一分子，同时结合5种毒素？ Claude提醒他们，成功概率很低。5种毒素虽然同属蝎毒神经毒素，但表面结构、关键位点、电荷分布和空间构象都有差异。想用一个小蛋白同时匹配多个靶标，相当于让一把钥匙打开五把结构不同的锁。 团队还是决定试一试。 这一步很有象征意义。AI可以让门外汉进入蛋白设计流程，但生命科学的难度不会因为提示词变长就自动消失。 35页提示词，300多个Agent，1万小时H100 真正开始前，Citrini和Anthropic团队花了大量时间设计提示词。最终形成的提示词长达约35页，里面写清楚了目标毒素、设计约束、评估工具、筛选规则、候选分配和实验室所需信息。 这已经不像普通聊天，更像一份交给“虚拟干实验团队”的研究计划书。 随后，Claude开始接管大部分计算设计流程：查文献、调工具、做结构预测、管理计算资源、筛选候选方案。它还在人类监督下给Twist Bioscience的科学家写邮件，询问某些融合蛋白和双特异性构型能否制造。收到回复后，Claude再把供应商的制造约束写回设计流程，继续推进。 这一点很关键。真实科研从来不只存在于论文和模型里，还要经过供应商、制造限制、实验排期、样品制备等现实环节。Claude能把这些信息串起来，项目才有了完整工作流的样子。 根据Citrini披露，整个设计活动用了略多于10000小时H100 GPU。算力费用49997美元，Claude甚至比预算少花了3美元。后续DNA合成、蛋白表达纯化、结合测试和可开发性评估等实验费用接近15万美元。20万美元预算基本花满。 在64小时设计阶段里，Claude生成超过31万个蛋白设计，筛出180个。经过后续四轮跟进，人类与Claude又补充了一批候选，最终211个方案被送往实验室合成和测试。 Citrini团队后来回忆，第一次在屏幕上看到蛋白结构图时，感觉很不真实。几天前，他们还在做投资研究；几天后，屏幕上已经出现了一批前所未有的蛋白结构，旁边还有排序、理由、制造建议和实验提交材料。 这正是AI for Science变化最直观的地方。专业能力开始被拆解成工具链： 大模型负责理解目标、调度流程、整合文献、生成设计；外包实验室负责验证；人类负责设定问题、监督风险、判断方向。 211个蛋白送进实验室，17个阳性结果，覆盖5种毒素中的4种 计算机里的结构图再漂亮，也不能算科学结果。C itrini把候选方案送到Adaptyv Bio和Twist Bioscience，进行DNA合成、蛋白表达纯化和结合测试。实验结果显示： 211个送测设计中，17个达到预设结合标准，覆盖5种毒素中的4种。 其中，针对墨西哥蝎毒Cn2的候选表现最突出。Cn2-B1和Cn2-B2两个设计与目标毒素结合很强，亲和力达到低纳摩尔级别。通俗讲，这意味着它们“抓得很紧”。在药物发现早期，这类亲和力已经足以让研究人员认真对待。 团队还做了竞争结合实验。已知有一种抗体片段LR可以中和Cn2毒素。实验显示，当LR先占住毒素后，Claude设计蛋白与毒素的结合受到明显影响。这提示Cn2-B1、Cn2-B2可能抓住了与LR相同或相邻的位置。 这很重要。抗蝎毒蛋白真正要做的事情，不能只是在任意位置贴住毒素，最好能挡住毒素与神经细胞钠通道作用的关键区域。竞争实验至少给出了一条积极线索： Claude设计出的蛋白，可能抓到了有功能意义的位置。 同时，最难的“通吃五种毒素”目标失败了。没有任何设计被证明可以同时结合多种毒素。Claude最初的风险提示应验。 这个结果反而让案例更可信。AI没有魔法般跨过所有生物物理限制。它在单一靶标上交出实验阳性候选，在多靶标通用分子上撞到墙。成功和失败都清楚地落在实验数据里。 还没变成药，但已经越过一道门槛 目前这些蛋白只证明了“能结合毒素”。它们还没有证明能中和毒素，也没有证明能保护细胞、动物或人体。 下一步需要功能实验。比如先确认毒素确实会扰乱细胞离子通道，再用patch-clamp等方法测试这些蛋白能否阻止或逆转毒素作用。之后才可能进入动物保护实验，评估剂量、起效速度、体内停留时间、安全性、免疫反应和制造稳定性。 换句话说，距离真正可用的抗蝎毒治疗方案仍有很长距离。 但这次实验的价值已经出现：一群几乎没有药物研发背景的人，在AI工具、实验外包和专家安全框架帮助下，可以从一个投资问题出发，走到“部分实验验证的新蛋白”这一步。 Citrini没有变成传统意义上的生物技术公司。它依然是一家投资研究机构。但它用20万美元和3个月时间摸到了一条新边界： 科学发现的入口正在被重新打开。 AI制药进入下一阶段 把Citrini的故事放在AI制药行业的大背景里看。过去几年，AI制药经历过一轮高预期。市场曾期待AI直接缩短新药研发周期、显著降低成本、快速推出重磅药物。现实更复杂。药物研发的瓶颈很多：靶点选择、分子设计、成药性、毒性、临床入组、制造放大、监管审批，每一关都可能让项目停下来。 因此，AI制药接下来的进展，大概率不会体现为某个模型“一步生成新药”，更可能体现在研发链条的多个环节被持续压缩。 Anthropic展示的是大模型协调蛋白设计流程的能力；Radical Numerics把AI设计噬菌体推进到耐药菌感染患者的同情用药场景；OpenAI通过Rosalind和Orchestra Bio，把AI延伸到科研项目管理、实验依赖追踪和研发流程协调。 这三类能力拼在一起，正好对应AI制药的三个关键方向：设计分子、验证生物功能、管理复杂研发系统。 Citrini案例给行业的启发尤其直接：AI制药未来的参与者可能会更多元。药企、CRO、顶级实验室依然重要，但越来越多带着具体问题、具体资源、具体判断的人，也可以进入科学工作流。他们未必会独立完成全流程，却能提出被忽视的需求，组织工具和实验资源，快速形成可验证结果。 这会改变早期研发的供给方式。过去，一个冷门疾病或边缘公共卫生问题，很难吸引大药企投入。现在，如果AI能够降低早期探索成本，小团队就有机会先跑出实验信号，再吸引基金会、政府、药企或产业资本接力。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 看好明年需求，宁德时代还要回答哪些问题？
articles.summary: 10月20日晚，宁德时代管理层称，明年全球动力及储能电池需求增长两至三成，是“可达到而且不算很高”的预期。 十几个小时后，宁德时代A股低开5%，盘中跌幅一度超过10%。 10月20晚的业绩会上，公司解释了三季度为什么卖出更多电池，却没赚到更多毛利。但当推向四季度，盈利改善的时间和幅度仍有变数。 四季度最先要检验的是单位盈利。新增税费的分担尚未谈妥，高毛利新品能补上多少，也要靠实际销售来证明。与此同时，部分车企正自己定义电池，并可能据此增加供应商选择，宁德时代需要守住订单和议价空间。扩产还在继续，新工厂的订单衔接和储能项目的交付速度，又会影响成本与资金回收。 宁德时代对需求的乐观，与机构的判断并没有那么远。小摩同样预计明年全球动力及储能电池需求增长20%至25%，但更担心车企自身盈利承压，消费税、出口退税调整等新增负担，会更多留在供应链。 三季报已经显露出这种压力。当季宁德时代归母净利润212.46亿元，同比增长14.54%，环比下降5.77%。收入比二季度增加约174亿元，毛利总额却近乎不变，毛利率从23.15%降至20.69%。税金及附加、资产减值损失合计环比增加约27亿元，研发费用也在上升。 管理层将单位盈利下降的首要原因归于产品组合：三季度交付了更多制造相对简单、附加值较低的产品和项目。同样的电量，以电芯、电池包或整套系统交付，利润并不相同，客户和合同也会带来差异。公司认为，这些因素对当季盈利的影响，大于税费变化。 产品组合可以随交付调整，新增税费却要与客户重新协商。管理层承认，产业链各方都有盈利压力，消费税的分担比例还没有谈定。三季度只受到一个月的影响，四季度则覆盖整个季度。这也意味着，即使交付结构改善，成本分担的结果仍会影响盈利修复。 车企自研，又让这场谈判多了一层变化。 理想采取电池包自研自制、电芯自研代工的分工；小鹏汽车董事长何小鹏则表示，小鹏开始自己做电池，但不做电芯。车企仍需要专业电芯厂，但开始更深地介入产品定义和系统集成。 对宁德时代而言，留在手里的订单也可能面临重新定价。客户若能按自研方案组织供货、增加供应商选择，宁德时代就更需要证明，技术、质量和交付优势值得客户多付钱。 宁德时代管理层引用的数据显示，前八个月全球动力电池份额仍同比提升1.7个百分点至39.4%。规模优势尚在。接下来客户自研车型实际交付多少、原有供应商的采购份额如何调整，比“去宁”的口号更能说明这种变化的影响。 储能和海外业务能提供多少有利润的增量，也因此更受关注。管理层称，三季度储能销售增速仍快于动力，海外需求旺盛；谈及国内时，也回应了市场对装机与提货差距、渠道库存的疑虑，认为明年国内储能增速可能没有市场想象的高。 订单转成业绩，还隔着交付和验收。管理层介绍，部分海外交流侧项目从发货到确认收入，需要半年至一年甚至更长；国内提货与装机之间的差距，则关系到客户后续还有多少补库需求。 宁德时代继续扩产，有眼下的订单作为依据。上半年，公司产能利用率达94.86%。管理层称，三季度新增产能缓解了供应紧张，排产和交付仍同比、环比增长。 但半年末764GWh在建产能陆续投产后，需要更大的订单规模。现有工厂的高利用率，无法直接推算新工厂的回报。面对2027年、2028年订单能否跟上扩产的追问，管理层强调以实际需求为依据，没有给出新增产能的订单覆盖比例。产能投放之后的利用率、库存周转和回款，会比在建规模本身更有说服力。 为了接住明年的需求，宁德时代已经先拿出了钱。 三季度，公司经营现金流净额从二季度的265.36亿元降至14.09亿元。采购付款环比增加342.41亿元，远高于销售回款57.50亿元的增量。同期购建固定资产等长期资产支付现金约170.95亿元，当季经营净现金流已不足以覆盖。季末超过4300亿元的货币资金及交易性金融资产，为这些投入提供了支撑。 宁德时代管理层解释，公司响应行业账期支付规范倡议，增加预付款、缩短账期，并支持供应商研发，帮助受资金约束的核心供应商准备产能和物料。这类支持预计持续两至三个季度。“今年下半年是为明年做准备的一个时间段。” 这些付款首先改变了现金支出的节奏。账期调整稳定之后，交付和回款能否跟上，才会逐步显现这轮投入的效果。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 高盛四张图推了三大资产：铜、金和电网
articles.summary: AI扩张、能源转型与央行囤金，三股需求浪潮正撞上各自的供给瓶颈。 高盛在最新大宗商品报告中，用四张图为铜、黄金和电力市场构建了一套结构性看多逻辑。 高盛大宗商品团队在最新报告中点名三个市场—— 铜、黄金以及以PJM为代表的特定电力市场 ——认为这三个领域均已出现需求加速与供给受限的正面碰撞。这不是短期地缘溢价的故事，而是一个供给响应以年计、需求增长以季计的结构性错配。 在核心预测上，高盛预计 LME铜明年均价将达每吨15400美元 ，较去年不足10000美元的水平大幅跳升，较当前现货价高出约7%； 黄金目标价则维持2027年底5400美元不变 。电力方面， PJM市场的前瞻电价已从过去十年的每百万英热单位约2至3美元跃升至约10美元 ，数据中心需求是核心驱动力。 值得注意的是，这一判断并非高盛独家。据悉，瑞银将铜列为其“最高确信度”主题，美国银行亦在押注铜与铀，多家机构正从不同角度指向同一个供给稀缺的结构性叙事。 铜：电气化与AI叠加，供给端无力跟上 高盛将铜的看多逻辑建立在多重需求驱动之上：电气化、能源安全、准战略性囤货、数据中心与AI基础设施建设，而矿山供给则被描述为"相当受限"。 铜的价格信号已经出现。铜价曾于9月8日创下历史新高，实体经济开始为稀缺性重新定价。 更关键的细节在于库存结构。高盛指出， 美国以外地区的可见铜阴极库存已降至季节性低点 ，原因是美中两国正在争夺有限的全球供给。关税不确定性持续将金属吸引至美国仓库，进一步收紧了LME定价所在的美国以外市场；与此同时，中国收紧废铜发票核查规则，迫使加工商转向阴极铜，进一步消耗中国国内阴极库存。高盛预计这一动态将在未来一年内持续。 黄金：央行购金节奏是核心变量 黄金的结构性驱动逻辑同样清晰，但短期存在下行风险。 高盛承认， 9月份黄金看涨期权需求的下滑——背景是美联储降息预期调整、"货币贬值"叙事降温——意味着其2026年底4650美元预测存在下行压力。 然而，高盛认为结构性驱动因素并未改变。 核心假设是：央行将以过去12个月约每月60吨的速度持续购金，贯穿2026至2027年。 这一速度是2022年前17吨月均水平的逾三倍，而这一体制性转变的起点，正是2022年俄罗斯外汇储备遭冻结事件。 报告称，储备管理者为何偏好实物黄金而非账面资产，答案已不言而喻——他们正越来越倾向于持有可以实际掌控的储备。 PJM电网：AI热潮撞上基础设施天花板 电力市场是这份报告中最具现实紧迫感的部分。 PJM覆盖美国13个中大西洋州，其中包括弗吉尼亚州——"全球数据中心之都"。 数据足以说明问题： PJM数据中心装机容量从2012年的约2吉瓦增长至如今逾20吉瓦 ，增幅超过十倍。PJM目前约占美国数据中心总容量的38%，以及全球数据中心容量的六分之一。 供需失衡已直接反映在电价上。 PJM前瞻12至23个月电价（扣除天然气成本后）已从过去十年大部分时间的每百万英热单位约2至3美元，跳升至约10美元。 电网压力已引发政策层面的直接干预。美国能源部已于10月13日下令PJM调度备用电力以维持供电稳定。高盛的结论是：对于超大规模数据中心运营商而言，答案在于自建发电能力——当下是表后电源，未来是小型模块化反应堆，而非继续排队等待一个已经满负荷运转的公共电网。 底线：供给以年计，需求以季计 高盛报告的核心逻辑可以用一句话概括： 在需求持续上升遭遇供给长期受限的市场中，结构性价格上行压力将持续存在。 铜矿从勘探到投产需要十年以上；黄金产量增长极为缓慢；电网扩容受制于审批、材料与工程周期。而AI算力需求、能源转型投资与央行购金行为，均在以远快于供给响应的速度推进。 正如高盛所言： 芯片、赤字和数据中心可以印出来，但铜矿、金条和变电站印不出来。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: Ken Griffin详解“AI大跌”：算力类似航空，“边际定价”、“折旧期限”与“企业预算”三大陷阱
articles.summary: 10月21日，在Citadel年度全球市场未来峰会上，Griffin接受彭博记者Dani Burger采访时表示，市场正从过去两年的"主题式扫货"转向真正意义上的基本面研究。他说："我认为这个市场正在经历的，是人们真正开始做功课。" 过去两年，市场逻辑简单粗暴：数据中心万亿级建设潮开启，买入全产业链卡位节点——英伟达、高带宽内存DRAM、超微多层陶瓷电容器MLCC，以及韩国、中国台湾、日本供应商和云计算巨头——几乎稳赚。如今，这套逻辑正在被重新审视。近日，AI交易也遭遇大幅重挫， 半导体板块遭遇了金融危机以来最长连跌。 Ken Griffin警告：GPU与航空公司高度相似，边际运行成本极低，一旦算力供过于求，现货租赁与API调用价格将瞬间崩塌，重演2000年电信泡沫中"暗光纤"的覆辙。 陷阱一：边际定价崩塌——GPU的“航空公司时刻” Griffin用航空业打了一个直接的比方。 "GPU和航空公司非常相似，边际运行成本极低。航班上有一个空座，哪怕只卖20美元，那个座位也是赚钱的。"他说，"正是这一特性决定了，一旦航空公司出现运力过剩，定价就会自由落体。" 他随即将这一逻辑延伸至算力市场："如果我们到达一个GPU供给超过需求的节点，边际定价实际上将会自由落体。" Griffin援引2000年电信泡沫作为历史参照：当年大量铺设的光纤，因需求不足从未被点亮，成为"暗光纤"，电信价格随之直线下跌。他的问题是：算力市场是否正走向同一条路？ "这将彻底颠覆人们今天所依赖的所有投资假设。这是第一个问题。" 陷阱二：折旧模型失效——“有用寿命”被高估 Griffin提出的第二个问题，直指投资机构的估值模型。 "现在有人用5至6年前的老旧GPU，依然能收取极高的租金。这种情况在未来5至6年里大概率不会持续。"他说，"因此，越来越多的人开始担忧：我不能再像12个月前那样，对一块芯片的第七、八、九年给予同样的资本化率或收入模型。" 换言之，若投资机构仍按7至9年的高资产残值进行折旧贴现，其估值模型将面临系统性重估压力。 陷阱三：企业预算收紧——ROI精算时代来临 Griffin指出，企业端的AI支出逻辑已经发生根本转变。 "美国最精明的企业，正在变得非常清醒——哪些业务需要为OpenAI和Anthropic的顶尖模型支付极高价格，哪些业务可以用开源模型以极低成本运行。" 他补充道："如果你看看那些在内部真正用好AI的公司，它们正在迅速变得非常善于最大化每一分AI支出的回报。我认为整个企业界都在看着来自Anthropic和OpenAI的账单，然后说：好，我们需要想清楚，怎么确保我们真的从中获得了生产力。" 7500亿美元与企业缩减账单的正面碰撞 这一企业端收紧趋势，与AI大模型公司的扩张计划形成了直接矛盾。 据《华尔街日报》报道，Anthropic在其S-1文件中披露，未来计划投入7500亿美元算力开支，且支出规模仍在增加。 记者Dani Burger直接问Griffin：这两件事之间是否存在张力？ Griffin的回答简短而直接："是的。你在提问的时候就已经回答了这个问题。" 他随后指出，问题的关键在于Anthropic能否将自身模型打造成"必需品"——例如在生命科学领域，若其模型真正能够帮助攻克癌症或其他致命疾病，那么每家制药公司都将不惜任何代价购买其技术。"但我们现在不知道答案。" 泡沫之问：历史总是相似，但结局未必相同 对于市场上日益升温的"AI泡沫"讨论，Griffin给出了一个有历史纵深的回答。 "在这个时刻，几乎可以肯定存在局部泡沫。任何对经济的根本性变革，通常都与泡沫交织在一起。"他说，"我只希望我当年留住了亚马逊的股票。" 他的判断是：泡沫破裂后留下的，往往是改变世界的技术基础设施，而穿越泡沫的公司，将成为未来数十年的市场领导者。 但他同时强调，这并不意味着当下的定价风险可以被忽视——尤其是在边际定价、折旧假设和企业预算这三个维度上，市场的重新定价才刚刚开始。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 谷歌CEO最新访谈：云业务正在为前沿AI“让路”，客户想锁定明年的算力“极难”，RSI“距终局还很远”
articles.summary: 近日，谷歌发布旗舰模型Gemini 4 Argon，这款模型在72小时内消耗了25万亿Token，是上一代Gemini 3.0同期的三倍，并创下谷歌历史纪录。 谷歌CEO皮查伊（Sundar Pichai）在模型发布后的首次公开深度访谈中，正面回应了外界关于“谷歌放弃前沿AI”的质疑，并罕见承认公司云业务正在为前沿模型研发主动让渡算力资源。 皮查伊坐进硅谷山景城的录音棚，接受科技媒体人Alex Kantrowitz主持的《Big Technology Podcast》专访。他证实了全行业算力严重短缺的判断——当下每家公司的实际需求都是两年前规划产能的2倍，客户今天想锁定2027年的算力“极其困难”。在递归自我改进（RSI）问题上，皮查伊明确划定边界：当前阶段是AI智能体与人类研究员协同推进的过渡期，距离“自主失控的终局”仍相当遥远。 前沿模型，是谷歌的“第一优先级”，不是选项 过去一年，硅谷流传着一种颇具市场说服力的逻辑： 前沿大模型的军备竞赛已经进入边际收益递减区。Meta的Llama系列开源模型、谷歌自家的Gemini Flash这类轻量快速模型，对绝大多数企业场景已经“够用”。既然如此，谷歌何必继续烧上百亿美元去卷万亿参数的前沿模型？不如把TPU算力全部高价出租给外部开发者，做下一个英伟达。 这种论调在投行报告和企业CTO圈子里流传甚广，甚至一度形成了“谷歌实际上已经战略性放弃前沿竞争”的市场预期。 皮查伊在访谈中对这个逻辑做了正面反驳，但他的切入角度并非情绪性的否认，而是从三个具体机制展开： 第一个机制是“早看见”的优势。 处于前沿的公司能比其他人更早观察到涌现能力，从而更早为下一代技术做准备。这是一种信息优势，而非单纯的性能优势。 第二个机制是RSI（递归自我改进）。 在用模型来开发下一代模型的时代，前沿模型的质量直接决定了下一代模型的天花板。用一个性能平庸的模型来搭建研发流水线，相当于用低精度工具来制造精密仪器——误差会逐层放大。 第三个机制是内部验证。 Argon上线后，谷歌内部开发者的使用数据给出了直接证据： 我们在内部已经清楚地看到了一个陡峭的拐点，把Argon部署给我们的开发者之后，它能解决我们以前的模型根本做不到的问题。 皮查伊还给出了一个具体数字：Argon上线四周内，谷歌内部代码销售量提升了30%，代码回滚率下降了约三分之一。这意味着工程师不仅写得更快，还写得更准——这是一个质量提升的信号，而非单纯的效率指标。 对于模型“够用论” ，皮查伊的态度是承认小模型的价值，但划清了边界： 各种尺寸和能力的模型都有存在的空间，我们一直是这样做的，这也是为什么我们做了Flash、Flash Light等等。我同意你可以用不一定是最前沿的模型来构建很好的产品体验，因为前沿模型往往更慢也更贵。但我们在乎前沿的进展，我们致力于把所有这些都做好。 算力账本：云业务正在为DeepMind让路 这是整场访谈信息密度最高的一段，也是皮查伊最罕见的一次公开表态。 理解这段话需要先搞清楚一个结构性矛盾：谷歌同时扮演着两个角色—— 一个是烧钱冲AGI的前沿AI研究机构（Google DeepMind），另一个是靠出租算力赚高毛利收入的云服务商（Google Cloud）。这两个角色在算力这个最稀缺的资源上，存在直接竞争。 华尔街的逻辑是：每一块TPU拿去给DeepMind训练模型，就少了一块能对外出租赚钱的算力。在资本开支居高不下、短期云收入增速承压的财报季，这个矛盾被反复放大。 皮查伊在访谈中直接说清楚了谷歌内部的优先级排序： 我们的基本出发点，是确保我们投入足够的算力来保持在AI前沿的地位。这是不可谈判的，其他一切都在这个基础上运作。 更进一步，他承认了外界长期猜测但从未得到CEO级别确认的事实——云业务确实在为前沿AI研究做出让步： 我们的云业务在任何给定时刻，都在为了支持前沿AI开发而放弃短期收入，因为我们在做算力上的取舍。所以你说的那种情况，已经是现实了。 这句话的分量在于：它不是一个未来的战略承诺，而是对当下现状的描述。谷歌云在实际运营中，已经在系统性地压缩对外出租算力的规模，以保证DeepMind的研发需求。 但皮查伊也补充了一个反直觉的判断——适度的资源约束对研究本身未必是坏事： 就算是我们的AI研究员，一定程度的约束其实也是好事，那是激发创造力的来源，那是促使你想出更高效的算法突破、比如用更少内存的来源。 这段话背后是一个更深的逻辑：无限算力不等于无限进步，资源约束有时会倒逼出更根本性的架构创新。 算力危机：2027年的配额，“极其困难” 访谈中，主持人Kantrowitz提到了一个在硅谷风投圈广泛流传的信息——知名风投a16z联合创始人Ben Horowitz在播客中转述亚马逊CEO安迪·贾西（Andy Jassy）的话，称云算力已经"卖空到2028年"。皮查伊的回应，是迄今为止对这一说法最直接的CEO级别确认： 我觉得这个说法是合理的……如果今天有客户来找我们要2027年的算力，那是极其困难的事情。 为什么会到这一步？皮查伊给出了一个清晰的结构性解释：数据中心从决策到投产有2至3年的刚性滞后，而智能体任务的爆发完全超出了两年前的需求预测。 今天回头看，每家公司都是短缺的，不只是我们，其他公司也一样。大家都希望自己手里的算力是当初规划量的2倍。 皮查伊还补充了一个关键的时间锚点： 我们今天手里有的算力，是我们在2024年做的决策的产物。就算回到去年今天，智能体任务的爆发还没有发生。 这句话揭示了一个系统性问题：AI需求的增速已经超过了任何基础设施规划模型的预测能力。两年前做出的决策，在今天看来几乎必然是低估的。 对于“是否存在过度建设（overbuilding）”的追问， 皮查伊的回答是区分时间框架： 如果我拉一个足够长的时间框架，这个量级的建设对我来说完全合理。我们处于有史以来最重要的技术的早期阶段，这不像光纤——光纤铺完是暗的，没人用。我们是在每天都面临产能约束的情况下使用它。 他没有否认短期内存在局部过剩的可能——电力、内存、电工等2000多个配套要素中任何一个出现瓶颈，都可能导致局部积压。但他对长期需求的判断是确定性的： 我有没有信心，我们规划的算力最终会有用武之地？给足时间的话，绝对有。 RSI：不是智能爆炸，是“智能体和研究员一起干活” 递归自我改进（RSI）是这次访谈中技术密度最高的议题，也是当前AI安全讨论中争议最大的话题之一。 背景是：谷歌联合创始人谢尔盖·布林此前在一次DeepMind内部研究员圆桌上提到，Argon的核心创新之一是“更多地依赖模型来帮助开发模型”。这句话随即在AI安全社区引发了关于“智能爆炸”的讨论。 主持人Kantrowitz在访谈中直接抛出了这个问题，并提到了近期几起AI系统越权行为的案例。皮查伊的回应把RSI的当前状态拆解成了三个层次： 第一层：定义当前位置。 他明确指出，当前的RSI远没有到达科幻叙事中"自主失控"的终局状态： 在一个连续谱上，我们距离RSI的终态还相当遥远。今天正确的描述方式是：你有RSI循环，同时有AI研究员在模型开发的各个环节共同参与。我会说，你几乎是有智能体在某种自动化方式下，帮助AI研究员协同工作来构建这些模型。 第二层：安全机制。 他把安全框架描述为"纵深防御"——对齐研究是一层，但不是唯一的一层。在此之上还有实时遥测监控、沙箱隔离架构、以及给企业客户的部署控制权限。 第三层：行业标准化。 皮查伊把下一步的关键指向了跨行业标准建设： 就像金融控制领域有会计准则、有独立审计师一样，这些都是我们作为一个行业需要努力推进的下一步，包括使用独立评估机构进行评估的能力。 这段话的信息量在于：它承认了当前的对齐工作存在"明显缺口"，但将解决路径指向了外部标准化机制，而非单纯依赖各家公司的内部自律。 太空数据中心与长期下注 访谈的最后部分，皮查伊谈到了谷歌的几个长期战略赌注，其中最具想象空间的是太空数据中心项目。 谷歌已将TPU试验芯片送入太阳同步轨道，探索在太空中利用24小时不间断太阳能运行数据中心。在地面数据中心面临社区反弹、电网并网排队长达数年的背景下，这一方向的战略逻辑逐渐清晰。 皮查伊用Waymo的起点来类比这个项目当前的阶段： 这些技术让你想起那些时刻——你站在那里，它看起来有点像科幻，但你知道，10到20年之后，它实际上会以一种有意义的方式运转。 他透露，在访谈录制期间，团队正在等待太空中TPU的"Hello World"时刻——即首次成功运行的信号。 这个项目目前处于"两到三年"的早期阶段，而谷歌的量子计算项目已经走了将近20年。皮查伊对这类长周期赌注的态度，折射出谷歌在基础设施层面的时间观： 在太阳同步轨道上，以24小时不间断的方式获取我们能接触到的最丰富的能源形式，对于我们将要面对的算力指数级增长来说，这将非常有意义。 articles.title: 宁德时代回应市场担忧：行业需求没有那么悲观，接下来产能利用率仍将处于较高水平
articles.summary: 10月21日，宁德时代股价大幅下挫。A股盘中跌超10%，H股跌超9%，A+H股总市值降至1.1万亿元，成交额超160亿元。公司股价自2026年5月7日创出历史高点以来，累计回落已超50%。 此前一日， 宁德时代披露三季报 ：前三季度营收4421.37亿元，同比增长56.19%；归母净利润645.30亿元，同比增长31.60%。但第三季度单季净利润同比增速仅14.54%，低于营收增速，经营性现金流同比下降23.60%，引发市场担忧。 针对股价大跌背后的多项疑虑，宁德时代10月21日上午密集作出回应称，“行业需求没有那么悲观，接下来产能利用率仍将处于较高水平”。此外，三季度经营性现金流同比下降23.60%，系公司主动调整对供应商付款所致，公司称长远不影响现金盈利能力。 需求展望：2027年“依旧可以期待” 针对投资者对明年新能源行业需求的担忧，宁德时代表示，“从公司角度看，2027年行业需求依旧可以期待。” 公司逐一拆解各市场情况： 国内乘用车整体销量虽有所下降，但电动化率快速提升，单车带电量也在较快增长，“国内新能源乘用车动力电池的增速依然实现了正增长”；国内新能源商用车电动化率同样在快速提升；欧洲电动化趋势具有连续性，持续有竞争力的新车型推出；其他市场的电动化潜力"可能被市场低估"。 储能方面，公司称国内外均保持不错增速，“特别是海外部分市场的储能需求比较旺盛”。 公司总结称，“全球动力及储能电池的市场需求可能没有市场预期的那么悲观，仍有不错的增长潜力。” 产能利用率：高位运行，状态健康 对于产能利用率问题，宁德时代表示，上半年产能利用率“非常饱和”。 随着今年新产能陆续投产，产能紧张程度有所缓解。但公司同时指出，市场需求也在持续增长，“整体而言，接下来产能利用率仍将处于较高水平，保持较健康的状态。” 经营现金流下降：主动支持供应链所致 三季度经营性现金流同比下降23.60%，是此次财报引发市场关注的核心指标之一。 宁德时代对此给出解释：近几年锂电供应链上游企业现金流压力较大，公司从第三季度起主动调整对供应商的付款安排，“优先支持有研发能力、创新精神、积极配合公司扩产的合作伙伴”，具体措施包括缩短账期、支付预付款、提供研发资金支持等。 公司表示，上述措施“可能会持续一段时间”，目的是“推动产业链更健康、可持续的发展”。 对于市场最关心的影响，公司明确表态： 经营性现金流可能会有阶段性影响，但从长远来讲，不会影响公司的现金盈利能力，未来会回到相对健康的水平。 存货增加：发出商品为主，周转正常 三季度存货环比增加同样引发关注。宁德时代解释，存货金额增大是“随着公司业务规模发展带来的”，但“近几个季度公司存货周转天数一直相对稳定，并没有销售不畅或出货不畅的情况，属于正常存货周转”。 从结构看，增长的主要是发出商品，“未来会逐渐体现为公司收入”。 公司还补充，储能业务正从销售电芯和直流侧产品向提供交流侧和系统产品延伸，产品形态更为丰富，但“相应的交付和确认收入周期比之前有所延长”，这也是存货阶段性增加的原因之一。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 谷歌CEO：算力天天不够用，哪来的AI泡沫？
articles.summary: 谷歌CEO认为，当前AI领域并不存在过度建设的泡沫，因为算力每天都处于紧缺且被充分利用的状态；从长远来看，所有规划的算力最终都会被完全消化，因此谷歌将坚定投资，甚至不惜牺牲部分短期利润，以确保始终处于AI技术的最前沿。

articles.title: 马斯克：AI算力不愁卖，SpaceX明年6个月能回本
articles.summary: 马斯克在SpaceX电话会上表示，超智能算力将长期短缺，因此他主张签短期合同。眼下各大云厂商和数十家小公司追着要租算力，全答应能租出好几倍，明年回本周期做到六个月也不是不可能。
